newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico trade, current account ledger healthy.
newsitem.headline: Mexico trade, current account ledger healthy.

text.p: A healthy January trade surplus shows Mexico is so far ducking balance of payments troubles similar to those that dealt the economy a knockout blow in 1994.

Mexico revised its trade surplus for the first month of the year to $460 million from a previously released $329 million, the government said on Thursday. Economists had not expected the surplus to be revised up sharply.

"Good news. This is telling us we still have some breathing room on the trade balance even though the economy is strong right now," said Carlos Rosales, economist at Mexico's Grupo Financiero Bancomer.

The January trade figures overshadowed what might have otherwise been negative news on Thursday that Mexico's current account deficit in 1996 grew to $1.762 billion -- at least a few hundred million larger than expected.
The deficit was only slightly larger than the $1.578 billion deficit racked up in 1995, although that figure was revised from a previously released $716 million.

Despite the fact that the current account deficit had grown, economists said it was not a problem and nowhere near as big as the $29 billion shortfall in 1994 that helped spark the peso crisis later that year.
"It was larger than expected...(but) bottom line is, it's not huge. It's really a hill of beans," said Gene Frieda, an economist at I.D.E.A. in New York.

As a percentage of GDP, the current account deficit actually fell to 0.5 percent from 0.6 percent, figures some economists said show the country's growing economy is not yet pressuring its balance of payments.
"Given the difference in the economy between 1995 and 1996, Mexico did well not to have a steeper decline in the current account," said Denis Parisien, an economist at Bankers Trust in New York.

Parisien said the figures were additional evidence that Mexico's recovery was mostly export and investment led. Had consumption played a big role, the import bill would have been higher and the current account deficit worse.
Real gains in the peso for much of the past year fed growing worries here among some economists and Mexican businessmen that the country's trade surplus would quickly turn to deficit.

Most economists agree that as the Mexican consumer recovers from the high interest rates and inflation that followed the peso crisis, however, consumption is likely to rise and imports outpace exports by year's end.
Parisien added that Februrary's trade figures will be important because January's numbers were skewed by a smaller number of working days, artificially lowering the number of exports and imports.
